title: USAID’s Destruction Left Nepal Dangerously Exposed
gist: After USAID's dismantling in 2025, Nepal faces twice-repeated catastrophic floods with a far smaller US response ($36M vs $130M+ after the 2015 quake) and discontinued flood-monitoring and preparedness programs. The article also notes weak local ownership, a $4.7B reconstruction bill, and other Western donors retrenching.

insights.claim: The US response to Nepal's 2026 floods is far smaller than after the 2015 earthquake: about $36 million versus more than $130 million, with an initial $500,000 contribution that a former top USAID official called embarrassing.
insights.speaker: Bibek Bhandari
insights.so_what: Smaller US humanitarian outlays shift disaster burdens to recipient governments and other donors.
insights.quote: Compared to the 2015 response, the difference is night and day

insights.claim: USAID was effectively destroyed in July 2025 after funding freezes and mass layoffs under DOGE, removing its Disaster Assistance Response Team capability that had performed search-and-rescue and building assessments in Nepal.
insights.speaker: Bibek Bhandari
insights.so_what: Loss of US first-response coordination raises tail risk of slower response in future disasters in aid-dependent states.
insights.locator: USAID was effectively destroyed in July 2025

insights.claim: The State Department says its response follows Nepali government requests and that reforming assistance has made US crisis response faster, and other officials argue the 2026 disaster was smaller than the 2015 quake.
insights.speaker: Bibek Bhandari
insights.so_what: The official counter-narrative frames cuts as efficiency; data on response speed will decide credibility.
insights.locator: U.S. State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott

insights.claim: SERVIR-HKH, a USAID, NASA and ICIMOD satellite-based hazard monitoring program, ended in January 2025 (its contract was reportedly due to run through 2026), halting upgrades and user engagement even though existing tools stay on ICIMOD servers.
insights.speaker: Bibek Bhandari
insights.so_what: Frozen tools degrade in usefulness and sustainability, increasing climate-hazard exposure in the Himalayas.
insights.locator: Funding cuts are already affecting disaster monitoring

insights.claim: USAID's Tayar Nepal program disbursed more than $30 million between 2020 and 2024, and a 2014 USAID-supported flood-warning system on the Kankai River basin largely prevented casualties.
insights.speaker: Bibek Bhandari
insights.so_what: Documented effectiveness of early warning makes its loss a quantifiable risk.

insights.claim: Climate-driven Himalayan hazards are increasing: ICIMOD identified 47 potentially dangerous glacial lakes in Nepal, India and China in 2020, and Nepal has suffered multiple floods and avalanches since August.
insights.speaker: Bibek Bhandari
insights.so_what: Rising glacial-lake outburst risk implies downstream infrastructure, hydropower and insurance exposure.
insights.locator: Climate change is making the Himalayas

insights.claim: Nepal's disaster authority estimates flood reconstruction at about $4.7 billion, around 65 percent for infrastructure, and the figure is likely to rise after the latest flooding.
insights.speaker: Bibek Bhandari
entities: National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority
insights.so_what: A large reconstruction bill strains the Nepali budget and raises reliance on multilateral and bilateral funding.

insights.claim: Nepali experts admit institutional memory is weak and technology transfer ended when donor projects ended, so programs lacked local ownership and were not continued after USAID left.
insights.speaker: Bibek Bhandari
insights.so_what: Donor-dependent public-sector capacity is fragile; sustainability plans are the key factor for aid efficacy.
insights.locator: Disaster risk reduction experts such as Gangalal Tuladhar

insights.claim: The UK and several European states are also prioritizing domestic needs over foreign aid, compounding the loss of USAID, and USAID's dismantling cut about $1 billion per year of climate and biodiversity funding across more than 100 countries (One Earth Partners).
insights.speaker: Bibek Bhandari
insights.so_what: Falling Western aid budgets point to a structural funding gap for climate adaptation in vulnerable states.
insights.locator: A report published in September by Washington
